extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent applicants and attorneys (particularly for software/AI/computer-implemented inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether computer-implemented / AI-related claims constitute patentable subject matter (technical solution) and meet clarity and inventive-step-related technicality requirements in the JPO and CNIPA practice. Focuses on when data-processing / model-training / software steps are treated as technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical solution (Article 2.2 Chinese Patent Law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution is the technical solution as provided for in Article 2.2 Chinese Patent Law, and constitutes the subject matter of patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solution must utilize technical means in conformity with the laws of nature and obtain a technical effect. Examples: measuring sugar content of preharvest apples by a portable near-infrared spectroscopic sensor (claims 1-2) and a prediction method that uses physical measurements and meteorological data plus machine learning to predict future sugar content (claim 3) are judged to be technical solutions because they (i) solve a technical problem, (ii) use technical means, and (iii) obtain technical effects. If these three elements are present, CNIPA concludes the subject matter constitutes patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Processed by a computer' as a determinative claim feature
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim states it is 'processed by a computer', examiners assess whether specific computing or processing of information depending on the intended use has been implemented by concrete means or procedures on which software and hardware resources cooperate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO: When 'processed by a computer' appears in the claim, list concrete computational steps to show cooperation of software and hardware; if present, the claim is likely an 'invention'. If the wording 'processed by a computer' is absent, the examiner must refer to the description and common general technical knowledge to assess whether the method is nevertheless processed by a computer. (See JPO analysis for the mathematical-model and CNN training examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete hardware-software implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: A method is regarded as an invention when information processing by software has been concretely implemented by using hardware resources (cooperation of software and hardware resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO repeatedly stresses that concrete implementation by concrete means or procedures (e.g., specific steps carried out by a computer: training models, performing convolutions, pooling operations, data acquisition steps) supports characterization as an 'invention' because it establishes a specific operating method of an information processing device. The guideline expects examiners to identify such concrete steps in claim text or description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the invention improve internal performance or cause technical change to the computer?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claimed computer-implemented process improves the internal performance of the computer or causes any technical change to its composition or function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA: If the computer is 'just a device to carry out the solution' and the establishing process neither improves the computer's internal performance nor causes any technical change to the computer's composition or function, the claimed method may be treated as non-technical (abstract mathematical method) and thus not a patentable technical solution. Contrast: where the method has specific technical associations with the internal structure or improves execution effect of hardware (e.g., selecting optimal training scheme to improve hardware execution), CNIPA finds technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical nature of data and processing steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the data processed in each step are technical (physical/image/meteorological/text/semantic data) and whether each step is closely related to achieving an accurate technical result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA and JPO accept claims where processed data have 'exact technical implications' (e.g., physical measurements, image data, meteorological condition data, semantic text data) and the steps are closely related to the technical objective (e.g., predicting sugar content, image recognition across sizes, enriching semantic information). If the data and processing are merely abstract (general feature values, tag values) without a specific application field, the claim may be treated as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must solve a technical problem and obtain a technical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed solution must solve a technical problem (not merely an abstract or mathematical problem) and obtain a technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should articulate the technical problem (e.g., how to collect sugar content on trees, how to recognize images of arbitrary size, how to enrich semantic info for QA) and identify the technical effect achieved by the claimed measures. JPO/CNIPA conclusions hinge on demonstrating both technical problem and technical effect tied to technical means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: abstract mathematical methods / mental activities (Article 25.1(2) Chinese Patent Law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions that are abstract mathematical model building methods or rules/methods for mental activities and that do not involve combination with a specific application field do not constitute patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA example: a method that merely increases the number of training samples and trains a mathematical model with feature and label values, producing an abstract classification model, is characterized as an abstract model building method and falls under rules/methods for mental activities per Article 25.1(2), thus not patentable. Examiners should evaluate whether processing objects, processes, and results are tied to a concrete application field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim clarity / title must indicate product vs process (Article 26.4 Chinese Patent Law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims (and their titles) must clearly define the extent of the patent protection sought; the title should indicate whether the claim is for a product or a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Claims titled 'Sugar content data' did not clearly indicate whether they were product or process claims; CNIPA found they 'do not define the extent of the patent protection sought in a clear manner' and thus do not comply with Article 26.4. Applicants were advised to modify the title to e.g., 'A collection method of sugar content data'. Examiners should check titles and claim wording for clarity of claim category and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of description and common general technical knowledge when claim wording is silent
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is silent about being processed by a computer, examiners must refer to the description and common general technical knowledge to assess whether the claimed method is nonetheless implemented by a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO guidance: When 'processed by a computer' is not explicitly found in the claim, the examiner assesses from the specification and common general technical knowledge whether the method is processed by a computer; if so, the same 'software-implemented technical solution' approach applies. This requires examiners to analyze the specification for indications of hardware cooperation or intended implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating technical association with hardware/internal structure supports patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventive-step/technicality assessment, showing specific technical associations with the internal structure of the computer system or that the method improves hardware execution supports finding of a technical solution
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA example (training-method case): the method 'has specific technical associations with the internal structure of the computer system, and improves the execution effect of hardware in the training process', yielding a technical effect that improves internal performance — thereby constituting a technical solution. Examiners should look for whether claimed measures change or optimize hardware execution, resource use, or internal arrangements.
